To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we determined crystal structures that characterize two Rec A-like XPB helices and discover a unique RED motif and implied conformation changes within a conservatied functional core.

we have determined the first crystal structures of an XPB helicases from an archaeon and a eukaryote and have used these to show that XPB unwinds DNA in a unique manner with implications for damage verification in nucleic excision repair.

we determined the crystal structure of an Archaeoglobous fulgidus XPBs homolog and that it contains a unique DNA damage recognition domain, a unique RED motif that is essential for helicase activity and a flexible thumb motif.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the molecular basis for the recognition of DNA damage and how it leads to the unwinding of the DNA helix.
understanding the molecular mechanisms of DNA repair, and the structural and functional characterization of the XPB helicases.
the molecular mechanism of the human XPB helicases.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the XPB helicases are the first to be shown to unwind DNA in the presence of a lesion.
the XPB helicases are the only known helicases that have a DNA damage recognition and a DNA mismatch recognition domains.
the XPB core is highly conserved and that the XPB helicases are capable of unwinding dsDNA containing a lesion, but not dsDNA lacking a lesion.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
XPB is not a simple helicase but rather a complex enzyme with an integrated damage recognition function that may be critical for its function in nucleotide excison repair.
we have solved a crystal structure for an Archaeal XPB homolog, and that this structure has revealed a number of conserved motifs that are important for DNA unwinding.

we have determined the crystal structure of the archaeal XPB helicases from A. fulgidus (AfXPB), A. veneficus (AvXPB), and A. thermophilus (AtXPB) that define a RecA-like XP helicase core structure with an additional DNA damage recognition domain.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the XPB helicases are highly specific for damaged DNA.
XPB helicases have an unusual ability to unwind DNA in a lesion-dependent manner, suggesting a role in damage verification during nucleotide excision DNA repair.
XPB is a DNA helicase with a novel substrate specificity that can be modulated by the presence of DNA damage.
